subject.title: Orange — Measure J (City of Orange Hotel Guest Tax Modification Measure)

text: Shall the measure updating the City of Orange’s existing Transient Occupancy Tax, a tax on persons occupying hotel rooms by increasing the tax rate from 10% to 14% for hotels with 11 or more rooms and applying the tax to online and other travel companies, generating approximately $3,000,000 annually for general City purposes including police, fire and emergency response, parks, and street and infrastructure maintenance, until ended by voters, be adopted?

A “Yes” vote on Measure J authorizes the City to amend the Transient Occupancy Tax by increasing the tax rate from 10 percent to 14 percent for hotels with eleven (11) or more accommodations, applying the tax online and other travel companies, and updating the tax to apply to the full amount charged to hotel guests, as provided in the ordinance.
A “No” vote on Measure J does not authorize those changes to the City’s Transient Occupancy Tax.

The City Council of the City of Orange is submitting Measure J to the voters for consideration at the November 3, 2026 General Municipal Election. If approved by a majority of the voters, Measure J would amend Chapter 5.16 of the Orange Municipal Code to update the City’s Transient Occupancy Tax (“TOT”), commonly referred to as the hotel guest tax. The TOT is imposed on the occupancy of hotel accommodations and is paid by hotel guests rather than by hotel operators. The ordinance would continue to require operators to collect and remit the tax to the City.

The measure would increase the TOT rate from 10 percent to 14 percent for hotels with eleven (11) or more accommodations. Hotels with ten (10) or fewer accommodations would continue to be subject to the existing 10 percent tax rate.

The ordinance would also update the City’s TOT definitions and apply the tax to the full amount charged to guests for accommodations, including amounts collected by accommodations intermediaries such as online travel or booking companies, as provided in the ordinance.

Revenue generated by the measure would continue to be deposited into the City’s General Fund and may be used for any lawful municipal purpose. The ordinance does not dedicate revenues to any specific purpose or program. Revenues may be used for City services, including public safety, emergency response, street and infrastructure maintenance, parks, libraries, and other municipal services.
The City estimates that the measure would generate approximately $3 million annually, although actual revenues will depend on hotel occupancy, room rates, and related taxable charges.

A “Yes” vote on Measure J authorizes the City to amend the Transient Occupancy Tax by increasing the tax rate from 10 percent to 14 percent for hotels with eleven (11) or more accommodations, applying the tax online and other travel companies, and updating the tax to apply to the full amount charged to hotel guests, as provided in the ordinance.
A “No” vote on Measure J does not authorize those changes to the City’s Transient Occupancy Tax.

strong: REBUILD ORANGE: STRONGER FINANCES. SAFER NEIGHBORHOODS.

text: Measure J is a simple idea: hotel guests should pay their fair share of taxes for City of Orange services because Orange residents should not bear the entire cost of serving hotel guests.

Every day, visitors staying in Orange hotels rely on our police officers, firefighters, streets, parks, and other public services. Measure J simply asks visitors to contribute more toward the community they enjoy.

Our major neighbors – Anaheim, Garden Grove, Santa Ana, and Tustin – all charge higher hotel taxes than we do. Even increasing to 14%, Orange will remain competitive with neighboring cities that already charge equal or higher hotel tax rates.
